subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from the remarks made last evening by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). He referred to his comments on the subject of racism inside and outside the House last Friday. [Translation]
I raise this issue with deep sorrow. I do not wish to belabour the point and would much rather put it to rest. [English]
Last evening in the House the Minister of Transport stated, and he repeated it, that he had not charged any member of the House with racism. He kept emphasizing it and returning to what he had said in the House on Friday. Last evening, referring to what he had said outside the House on Friday, in response to questions from me the Minister of Transport said the following, and I quote from page 3963 of Hansard:
I think that the hon. Leader of the Opposition is an honourable man. He will take my word that I never referred to the House. On the contrary, the only place where it is clear is here, and it is in Hansard. When I was talking outside the House-and some day I will say it openly-I excluded the House and I excluded the whole opposition, and I say that the debate did not take place on racism.
I have listened to the tape of what the minister said outside the House on Friday, and I quote him again in my admirable French:

The minister was speaking.
It means that I was here in 1965. So I have witnessed the Lamon-tagne affair, the Favreau affair, the Tremblay affair, and wherever there were French Canadians, they tried to attack them. And whom are they attacking now in the House? The Minister of Transport, Chretien, Yves Pratte. Right? Well, all I have done is indicate to them that we are aware of it. Because if you look up the oral question period for the past month, you will see that this is what is going on.

Mr. Speaker, I have to say that the minister was clearly referring to the House and to the question period. He said last evening that he was only referring to Mr. Fisher and an editorial in the Ottawa Journal, but they do not ask questions in the House of Commons. I call the attention of the Chair once again to the use of the words "en chambre". These remarks could only be interpreted by the viewers on television, the listeners on radio, especially French-speaking listeners and viewers, as meaning that in the opinion of the minister the opposition was trying to injure or destroy ministers because they are Francophone.

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: The charge is absurd: we have paid a fair amount of attention to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp), to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: Even Jim Richardson.

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: But I say that it is not acceptable for the minister to make that kind of statement outside the House and to pretend inside the House that his remarks outside the House about the question period were not made and did not relate to members of the opposition.

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext:
The minister is in this position, I submit: in the House he has not charged any member of the opposition with racism, but outside the House that is the only interpretation one can draw from his remarks. The listeners and viewers who heard him and believed him must believe now that Francophone ministers are under attack because they are Francophone. That amounts to a charge of racism and I think the minister will agree with me, otherwise he would not have gone to such lengths to ask me to believe, last evening, that he had never made any reference to the House when he spoke outside the House on Friday. I cannot accept, and I suggest that the House cannot accept, a minister taking one attitude in the House and another attitude outside on a question such as this.
One can never catch up with this kind of statement having been made to the public: that harm is done. But I believe the minister is an honourable man. When he said last evening that on Friday he had not referred to what was going on in the House, and when he said last evening that on Friday he had excluded the House specifically, he misled the House; but I do not say, and I do not believe, that he did it deliberately. I assume that he forgot precisely what he had said on Friday and that perhaps in his enthusiasm at that moment he got carried away outside the House on Friday.
But I do say that it is a breach of the privileges of the House for the minister to go outside the House and suggest to the public that members of the opposition are trying to injure Francophone ministers in the House during the question period, simply because those ministers are Francophone, and then to come back into the House and say that outside the House he never said any such thing. I repeat, I believe the minister is an honourable man, and I ask him to withdraw the inference in the charges that he made against members of all opposition parties last Friday

Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Acts
outside the House and which, last evening, he denied having made.
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister has committed a breach of privilege but my main concern is to have an end to this whole unhappy episode.

subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume you are accepting the question of privilege as presented. I shall therefore limit myself to a few brief comments. I believe the way in which the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has explained the facts is honest and I have no quarrel with it.
Mr. Speaker, when I rose on a point of order yesterday, I made it very clear that I did not feel that anyone had racist tendencies in this House, or tried to attack Francophones strictly because they are Francophones. That part, I believe, was made clear to the House yesterday. I believe the only point the Leader of the Opposition has made is that outside the House I inferred there were racist goings-on in the House. If that is the case, then I understand that he should link the two together and I am willing to withdraw my words without any restrictions. I am convinced that no one has attacked me in my duties as Minister of Transport because I am a Francophone, nor any of my colleagues, and the use of the word "House" had another meaning for me at that time. In any event, I am in the wrong and not my colleagues opposite. I have always understood that there are not just hon. members in the House. Be that as it may, I withdraw what I said and recognize that the Leader of the Opposition is right in his interpretation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. STANFIELD-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN YESTERDAY'S DEBATE
speechtext: In the circumstances, I am sure it is not necessary to prolong the matter by adding, although I should perhaps do so for the record, that the nature of the question of privilege raised by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was most interesting and important. As the House knows, it was not followed by a motion asking for action of the Chair. In any case, it seems to me that its intention or declaration was equally well met, and that would seem to have disposed of the matter finally and very forcibly.

Following a question asked in 1973 about the victims of thalidomide, the minister had suggested that he had already had talks with Canadian manufacturers of that drug, and that he hoped to be able to give details on the nature of the agreement in the near future. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very surprised at the hon. member's question, since I have already answered similar ones in the House in 1973, and I answered a question from the hon. member for Joliette a few weeks ago. speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-50 neither gives the government of Canada or the Minister of Agriculture any authority which it did not have before under the legislation which it is proposed to amend. It does not enable the government to stabilize the price of any agricultural commodity in any area in Canada in any new or more effective way, and any statement or insinuation to the contrary is not in line with the honourable behavior expected from a minister of the Crown. I think that the government should be called upon to insist that ministers observe the standards imposed by the rules of this House in their statements inside and outside of this House in relation to misleading interpretations of legislation as it exists.

March 11, 1975
3978____________________________________
Agricultural Stabilization Act

The House resumed, from Thursday, March 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-50, to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in the debate on Bill C-50 I question whether agriculture has ever been in a more vulnerable position in the Canadian economy than it is at the present time, and unfortunately we have a minister who seems to be unaware of the real problems facing agriculture. We have a minister telling people, especially urban people, that they will have to pay more for food. I am concerned that eventually urban people will take exception to some of the comments of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) because they will not want continually to be backhanded in the face as they have been in the past. They are a very generous people and they are willing to pay a fair price for produce. Unfortunately agriculture is in an extremely difficult situation because this government will not come to grips with the real problem facing our economy, and that is inflation.
The people who strike for higher wages are in no better situation after they have received those wages than they were before negotiations started, when there was a little more stability in our economy. At the present time there is no stability in the Canadian economy. The situation which now exists on the west coast is deplorable. The people who are on strike there will never catch up on wages they have lost. It is a vicious circle. We on this side of the House go from one minister to another in the cabinet, trying to obtain an answer as to what the government will do about it, and they say nothing. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) says that the government is patient and, hopefully, the parties will meet again this week. The government seems unaware of the complexity of the problems for the Canadian people in resolving the economic problems we are all facing.
Last year the minister responsible for the Wheat Board was very quick in getting into the confrontation when grain companies and farmers were going to have to pay the shot. But now it is a different story: we hear very little from that minister. By the same token we do not hear much from the Minister of Agriculture. I just cannot understand how some of the backbenchers on the government side of the House can be so naive. I should perhaps refer to the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac). He said that the minister and the government are responsible for the stability evidenced in the beef industry. All the hon. member would have to do is talk to some of the beef producers to find out exactly what is happening in the beef industry. He should go out on the farm and see what is happening.
The minister says that we have a subsidy at the present time which is taking care of the beef industry. But it is not. Why in the world do we have to have a subsidy which

pays the same amount to a producer who receives 55 cents for his beef as it does to the man who is getting 35 cents? This is not fair and it is not conducive to establishing a strong, viable beef industry in our economy. It is not good for the economy and it is forcing a great many people out of the industry. Eventually the consumer will suffer because the product will not be available.
The minister takes pride in his knowledge of agriculture. He says there have been previous ministers of agriculture who did not know the difference between a cow and a sow. I do not know whether he refers to the member from Calgary who is now in the other place, or the former member for Medicine Hat who is still in Alberta. However, I am sure there will be ministers of agriculture following this minister who will say that this minister laid an egg, not primarily because that is how the situation could be assessed, but because of the way he has mishandled CEMA from the very beginning.
There is no way our agricultural industry problems will be resolved by implementation of programs such as this stabilization bill. It has been suggested that it will not do much more than the measures already available to the Department of Agriculture and the minister. However, one of the things we must have is a responsible minister who recognizes the problem and takes action to resolve it. It has been brought to our attention that the minister knew a year ago last December that an egg surplus was developing under CEMA, but he was able to keep the lid on it until after the election. Then, of course, 28 million eggs were destroyed. The minister did not smell so good at that time.
The consumer resents this type of inaction and so does the producer because he suffers a lot. It is immoral to destroy food in a hungry world. I think the minister knows this, but he does not seem to be capable of coming up with a policy that will keep up with the production that Canadian agriculture is able to develop. The minister is a great promoter of marketing boards. I think they serve a useful purpose, but they must have the support of the Department of Agriculture if they are to function properly.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think Canada should try to develop a world food bank all by itself, but I do think there should be such a world bank to distribute food to the hungry people of the world. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), in his position as chairman of the International Monetary Fund, could work toward this end. If we increased production by only 1 per cent or 2 per cent and channelled that amount to a world food bank, it would be of some help. If the 1 per cent or 2 per cent fell back on the Canadian economy, however, it could wreck the agriculture industry, and certainly the morale of the producer if the surplus were to be destroyed.
From December 1, 1974, to January 11, 1975, 50 carloads of eggs were imported from the United States, and in the week of March 3, 1975, 12 carloads were imported. That creates a problem for CEMA, and unless it has the support of this government and the Minister of Agriculture it just cannot cope with these things. Already Newfoundland and British Columbia have suggested that they will leave

CEMA, and Alberta is considering holding a plebiscite on the question of whether to remain in the organization. No organization can operate efficiently in an atmosphere of indifference and indecision. It is up to the Minister of Agriculture to do something about it-but he is reneging on his responsibility to the industry and we will continue to have problems until he accepts his responsibility. I am just using CEMA as an example, Mr. Speaker. If the problems in that organization can be resolved, I believe the problems in other sectors of agricultural production can also be resolved.
The poultry population on January 1 of this year was 22,443,244 according to CEMA. According to the Department of Agriculture, however, it was approximately 26 million, and according to the production and marketing branch it was approximately 24 million. With this discrepancy in figures it is impossible to tally the total productive capacity. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) pointed out the problem of overproduction. Quebec increased production last year by 42 per cent over the previous year. Production as of February 8, 1975, was up 29 per cent over the same month in the previous year. This proves that we have the ability to produce in this country. But then the question arises, what are we going to do with the surplus? The government should be prepared to direct it into markets that are readily available in other parts of the world, but of course this would take a certain amount of organization.
For some time the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) has been urging the government to set up a program to help feed the hungry people of the world. We cannot do this at present, however, with marketing boards setting goals that are less than our domestic requirements. Much the same thing is happening in the dairy industry, Mr. Speaker. We import 50 million pounds of cheese and 50 million pounds of butter in a year because we are not up to our maximum production. Farmers cannot afford to take the chance of producing more in case there is not a market. We saw what happened in the beef industry and now many people are getting out of it. When the grain industry got into trouble, we had at that time a fairly viable meat industry, so many farmers switched. But they cannot switch back today.
I suggest that within two or three years we will see animals being raised on grass to a greater degree, as they were when most of us were girls and boys. This will probably mean they will go into the feed lots at 800 pounds or 1,000 pounds, so it will take a couple of years for them to get there. In the end, production will be down and we will be short of beef. We have not cut back on production at present, as has happened in the United States. They have 135 million head of cattle, compared to our 15 million head. A short time ago they had 150 million head, but they are getting it under control. Our count remains at 15 million. The selling price of beef, of course, has fallen and the minister should be prepared to do something about it.
Unless the cabinet supports the Minister of Agriculture, our difficulties in agriculture will continue. The minister suggested that he enjoys the support of the cabinet. I doubt it. Let me refer the House to what he said as recorded at page 3813 of Hansard for March 5, 1975:
Agricultural Stabilization Act
There is also a provision in the bill which some of my colleagues in cabinet suggest gives the Minister of Agriculture a blank cheque to support the food producers of the nation. Never before has agriculture and its representative in the cabinet, the Minister of Agriculture, been given that authority. But-
And this is a big "but".
-I want to remind members of the House that before the Minister of Agriculture is granted that authority, there is an inter-departmental committee made up of five departments which studies all things pertaining to agriculture before a decision is made. There also are five cabinet ministers who decide on anything we do. That has been the situation for some time in cabinet. They consider the matter before any major decision is made which affects not only the agricultural producers but also the consumers in this country. Anyone who says that is not so is not stating the fact.
The minister, in the main, repeated what we have said. He has not enjoyed the support in cabinet which he, as the representative of the agricultural industry, deserves. Without that support it will be impossible for agriculture to be established on a viable, sound basis. Let me refer the House to the manner in which the government announced its restrictions, a little less than two years ago, concerning the cattle industry and involving exports to the United States. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), not the Minister of Agriculture, made the statement which signaled the downfall of the cattle industry in Canada. It has been losing money ever since. Cattle producers have been forced to refinance time and again. At some point they will not be able to refinance, and that is when the cows will come home, to use a cliche, for Canadian agriculture.
Who announced the appointment of the new deputy minister of agriculture? I will not comment on the ability of the new deputy minister as time alone will show if he has any. The agricultural industry does not like the idea of the Prime Minister appointing a man of his own choice. There are many capable men in Canada who could have helped the Minister of Agriculture in that capacity. The industry regrets the retirement of Mr. Sid Williams. We all hope that his successor, even though appointed by the Prime Minister, will fill his boots. But, Mr. Speaker, they are big boots to fill.
The building of a strong, stabilized agricultural industry will place a heavy load on the Minister of Agriculture. For this reason we hope he will accept advice from my side of the House more readily than in the past. Why do I say this? Let me illustrate. About two years ago, when the government tried to introduce a crop insurance program which would work and be accepted by farmers across Canada, we, in an effort to be helpful, tried to move amendments. They were not accepted. What happened? Farmers availed themselves of the program on an "on again, off again" basis. Some farmers tried to build up their own protection; nevertheless, the program has not accomplished its announced aims. You cannot institute a program like that overnight. We knew this and tried to introduce amendments to the bill when it was before the House. If they had been accepted, it would not have been necessary for the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to bring before the House the present grain stabilization bill.
Some people think that crop insurance is different from stabilization. It is not necessarily so. Actually, insurance and stabilization are one and the same thing. Remember, Mr. Speaker, we are interested in maintaining a viable

Agricultural Stabilization Act
agricultural industry, an industry in which farmers show a profit. If they do not, they go broke. So it does not matter if you call the program crop insurance or stabilization; the objective is the same. We maintain that you do not need both programs, because with two programs you establish two bureaucracies, one under the Minister of Agriculture and one under the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
Imagine what would happen with two bureaucracies. Inspectors working for the Minister of Agriculture would look in farmers' bins to see how much grain was stored before authorizing a payment. After they had left, inspectors working for the minister in charge of the Wheat Board would come to the farm and look in the same bins. Bureaucracy would be compounded. Actually, that is what is wrong with this government-there is too much bureaucracy. One department does not communicate with the other and too many bureaucrats are maintained in their jobs at the expense of the taxpayer.
Too many bureaucrats in jobs force taxes up. Because taxes are high, people strike for higher pay. If taxes were lower, people would be content with less pay. At present there is a vicious circle. We should reduce costs all through the economic chain so that ordinary people would derive the benefit. As things now stand, with grocery bills climbing, and clothing and shelter costs escalating, people will strike for more pay. If we are to cure this situation we must begin at the top. I hope the Minister of Agriculture pays attention to what we on this side suggest, because we do not want to have to tell him in two years' time that he made a mistake.
The minister said that eggs will not be included in this stabilization bill. I went to some pains pointing out why it is necessary to resolve CEMA's difficulties. Unless we resolve those difficulties, I submit it will be difficult to resolve other agricultural problems. I pointed out that the figures of Statistics Canada, the Department of Agriculture and CEMA are all different: they all tell a different story. CEMA itself now says it cannot rely on the figures of the Department of Agriculture or Statistics Canada, and wants to establish its own intricate system of record keeping. Surely it is up to the Department of Agriculture to provide such figures and to introduce policies which will benefit producers.
Although our agriculture is regionalized, I think the federal Department of Agriculture should take on the job of selling and exporting agricultural commodities-with the support of the provinces, of course. That would not mean taking anything away from the provincial governments. Goodness only knows, nobody is a stronger supporter of provincial rights than I am, but in the selling of agricultural commodities I think the federal department can do a better job than the several and individual provincial departments. The Wheat Board sells most of our wheat; why should not the Department of Agriculture sell most of our agricultural produce? Why not let one department handle all selling, instead of having the departments of agriculture of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and other provinces send delegations to Japan and other countries? These delegations are costly. Costs are duplicated. Why can we not decide on the price of a commodity before it leaves Canada? We could use marketing boards to set the price, if you like. Uniform marketing efforts would

end the present dissatisfaction. These remarks apply equally to CEMA. Egg production is up in Quebec and down in other provinces, and egg marketing is in a mess. Until the Department of Agriculture gives more leadership, we shall not resolve these difficulties.
I was surprised to hear the minister say that wheat produced in Ontario will not come under the jurisdiction of this stabilization bill. The minister had better take another look at that, because he said Bill C-19 would cover wheat produced in Ontario; oats and barley, yes; but he said it would take care of wheat. However, it only takes care of 50 per cent of the wheat grown in Ontario. I am going to read some figures into the record. These were presented when the representatives of the Ontario Wheat Board were before the committee. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) was questioning Mr. Young, chairman of the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board. He asked:

Yes; about half the crop.
The Minister of Agriculture will have to examine the situation in order to have that included. I have spent considerable time expressing my opinion and the opinion of those I represent. We want to see the bureaucracy of government reduced. We want the expense of production reduced. That is the only way to have a viable agriculture industry in Canada. We must first attack the cost of production. Until we get rid of government bureaucracy we will not be able to accomplish this.
Talk to some representatives of the industries. In the dairy industry, for example, the creameries and milk retailers with labelling requirements have extra work forced upon them. In certain areas bilingual displays are required on products even though the people do not require it. This is an extra cost of production. Why must all the ingredients be listed, when in a great many cases it does not mean anything to consumers? They know the products they want, and they buy them. Why does the Department of Agriculture not set up a data bank in Ottawa? If anyone wants to know the ingredients of a particular product, he could obtain the information from the data bank. He could then determine whether or not he wanted to continue buying the product. Surely, with our modern-day technology, such a data bank could be established.
These are some of the areas in which the minister is lacking: he lacks imagination and he lacks support in

cabinet. Until this failure is overcome we will continue to have problems in agriculture. We are just jumping from crisis to crisis. That is the way it has been since I came to the House of Commons. The Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) agrees we have been going from crisis to crisis. The time has come for the operation to be run smoothly: if not, we are lost and I do not know what will happen: it will be a catastrophe.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is intended to be a very important piece of legislation. It cannot be otherwise since, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) says, it deals with the production of food, of what he calls "the mainstay of life". While it is a series of amendments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act which has existed since 1957, it will give that act a much wider and more far reaching impact than it ever had before. The bill's purpose is to provide farmers with "a guaranteed floor price" for agricultural commodities. This means the bill has an importance far beyond the boundaries of the agricultural community itself, making up as it does only some 6 per cent of our labour force. In fact, the bill has great significance for everyone in the country.
However, in my view, so far in this debate a number of questions of vital concern to every Canadian have not yet been clearly or fully answered. These questions are important to all individual Canadians as taxpayers and as consumers. It would appear that the government intends, through the amendments set out in Bill C-50, to use the Agricultural Stabilization Act much more frequently and more fully than was possible in the past. However, the Minister of Agriculture has given us no indication of what the broader and more frequent use of this legislation will cost the government and, therefore, all individual Canadians as taxpayers. In the 1973-74 fiscal year, the Agricultural Stabilization Board spent $143 million, through the estimates, on payments to farmers. The recently tabled estimates say that the forecast of the board's expenditures for the 1974-75 fiscal year will be more than $301 million. These estimates also propose expenditures for the board during the coming fiscal year in the area of $261 million.
Does this proposed expenditure in the 1975-76 fiscal year take into account the more frequent and extensive use of the Agricultural Stabilization Board program contemplated by Bill C-50? If so, why is less intended to be spent in the current one? Is it possible that in spite of what is promised to the farmer through this legislation, it will in fact not be used as fully as the Minister of Agriculture implies? However, if more than $261 million is to be spent, we should be told, even if it is only in a general way, how much the government expects this greater expenditure to be.
Another key question for all Canadians is how much will the application of Bill C-50 cost them, not only as taxpayers but also as consumers when they do their shopping for groceries. In other words, what effect will Bill C-50 have on food prices? Bill C-50 would authorize the government to set base prices for the wide range of agricultural commodities to which it applies in a way that would make these base prices higher than would be possible under the formula used in the existing law. A significant question for Canadians, as consumers, therefore, is what is the connection between these base prices and
Agricultural Stabilization Act
retail prices for both processed and unprocessed food? Will a base price set under Bill C-50 operate anything like the intervention price set by CEMA under the national egg marketing plan?
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the evidence before the special egg marketing committee established that the intervention price at which CEMA bought eggs from farmers was set at such a high level that it caused the retail price for eggs to be so high that it discouraged consumers from buying them. Is there a risk that Bill C-50 can cause situations with respect to those commodities to be supported under this new agricultural stabilization program similar to what took place recently with regard to eggs? I think this is a valid question, since the Minister of Agriculture said the following about the stabilization programs to be undertaken by the federal government under this new law:
None of these programs can work without proper supply management.
What does he mean by the term "proper supply management"? What commitment is the government making about the way supply management will be used to support the operation of the agricultural stabilization program? What will the government be doing to avoid the creation of situations with respect to other commodities to be covered under Bill C-50 like the one that arose in egg marketing?
At the same time, supply management generally has meant quotas, that is, the limiting of production. So far in this debate the government has not really attempted to answer the kind of question I raised in the House during the debate on the income tax bill. The question is: during this period when there is not just a shortage of food but actual starvation in many parts of the world, do we have an obligation to adopt policies of maximum food production no matter what the effect on market prices might be? Also, how would such maximum production be paid for, recognizing that the cost of such production cannot fall primarily on the farmer? To what extent could we afford this kind of policy at all?
Thus far in the debate no indication has been forthcoming as to the extent to which the bill before us may be part of a total food policy, or the degree to which the government and the Minister of Agriculture are committed to developing one. By a total food policy I mean a policy which deals not only with the role of primary producers but also, and equally, with the role of the others in the food chain-the processor, the wholesaler and the retailer. It is one which must include programs to encourage efficiency and productivity and also to review the pricing policies of those groups which operate beyond the farm gate.
The purpose of this bill is to protect farmers against having to bear alone the burden of receiving prices for their production when those prices from time to time are at their very lowest. But the government has said nothing, or at least very little, about what the rest of the Canadian population will actually be getting through Bill C-50, particularly in the vital area of prices. The government's silence in this area of policy, at least until this point in the present session, is not consistent with the commitment it

Agricultural Stabilization Act
gave the Canadian people in the Speech from the Throne of February 27, 1974, which said:
Guarantees against unduly low prices for producers must be coupled with guarantees against unduly high prices for consumers.
Does the government not have an obligation to follow through with concrete action on both sides of the equation-guarantees against unduly low prices for producers and guarantees against unduly high prices for consumers? So far, only the commitment to agricultural producers has been set out in terms of specific legislation, that is, in Bill C-50. There is nothing in this bill itself which will ensure the carrying out of the commitment to consumers which the government made with equal force in the throne speech of February, 1974.
However, there is already in existence a program with regard to a key agricultural commodity which is based on the kind of approach I am talking about, the approach outlined in the throne speech of February, 1974. I am referring to the government's program for two-price wheat which is being turned into legislative form through Bill C-19. This program assures western farmers that for some seven years there will continue to be a floor below which the price they get for their wheat cannot fall no matter how low world prices may tumble. At the same time, along with this protection government policy provides for a ceiling above which the price in Canada cannot rise. Thus, the wheat farmer forgoes the opportunity to get world prices when they are at their peak in return for being protected against receiving world prices when they are at their lowest. This policy provides mutual benefits for both farmer and consumer.
There is nothing of this approach in Bill C-50. It contains only the provision respecting floor prices for farmers, but nothing specific about an equivalent kind of protection for consumers through some kind of ceiling on the prices they pay for the commodities which will be covered by the new agricultural stabilization program. Has the government abandoned the commitment made to consumers in the February, 1974, throne speech? Canadians generally, I am sure, hope this is not the case. After all, this was the throne speech on which the government went to the people and sought re-election. This was the throne speech which formed an important part of the basis for the judgment people made in re-electing the government with a clear majority last July 8.
The Minister of Agriculture says Bill C-50 will encourage production. However, the bill is a series of amendments to the existing Agricultural Stabilization Act. The preamble of this act sets out that it is-
-for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income.
This preamble contains no reference to production, although providing farmers with a fair share of the national income is, generally speaking, an objective with which Canadians would be in sympathy. Questions can be asked as to the method the government intends to use to achieve this objective. Does the government intend to keep up retail prices for food by a combination of supply management limiting production and of base prices set

under Bill C-50? Or, will the government encourage greater production but use Bill C-50 to prevent the law of supply and demand from operating so that the greater production cannot create a downward pressure on retail prices to consumers, allowing them to benefit from the effect of this kind of market force? The Minister of Agriculture said, when he spoke at the beginning of this debate:
So long as we have properly planned programs such as this stabilization program it will cost the government hardly anything, if anything at all, in the long run. It will not cost the producers anything-
Well, to paraphrase the old song, most taxpayers will say that the expenditure of $261 million is "plenty of nothing." They are entitled to ask, on whom and in what way will the real cost of Bill C-50 actually fall? Such questions should be explored, since if the new bill is to be fully and actively used-and remember that only $261 million is allotted for it in the estimates-it could mean that the government intends that higher returns for farmers in respect of basic agricultural commodities will come primarily from the marketplace. But if this happens, the burden will not fall with equal fairness on all Canadians. The reason is that the burden of higher food prices in the marketplace falls most heavily on lower income consumers who spend a higher proportion of family income on foodstuffs.
This is a further argument for extending the floor and ceiling approach adopted in the two-price wheat program to other commodities. It is also an argument in favour of deciding that an appropriately larger part of the cost of the new agricultural stabilization program should be met through government expenditure since the funds for it come from taxpayers generally and are raised on the principle of ability to pay.
One can recognize and accept the importance and the justice of the concepts set out in Bill C-50, aimed, as they are, at sheltering the farmer from uncertainties caused by the state of world markets, alternating gluts and shortages of world production and varying weather conditions. However, the small businessman, the small manufacturer, the skilled tradesman, might well ask, "Why is there nothing like Bill C-50 for us?" They could argue that they, too, are self-employed, like the farmer, and that they face similar kinds of uncertainties. Nevertheless, the government is not giving them minimum prices for their production although it is asking them in one way or the other to help pay the cost of this kind of assistance for agriculture.
Of course, the answer may well be found in the importance of our agricultural sector to our country and to the world. If this is the case, it must be observed that agricultural spokesmen can hardly be justified in complaining, as they often do, about the attention being paid to agriculture today by governments, on behalf of the general public, through such measures as the Food Prices Review Board, the special parliamentary inquiry into egg marketing and various government programs. If agriculture has the importance its protagonists claim for it, then the over-all public interest requires that the government, on behalf of all Canadians, pay the same kind of attention to it that the government is expected to pay to other key sectors of the economy. Primary producers can hardly ask for wide-ranging support from the government and object
March 11, 1975

to scrutiny from government as to how their role fits in with the over-all public interest in terms of the government's priority obligation to protect that interest.
I have asked the kinds of questions I have raised today in a constructive and positive sense and in the belief that Bill C-50, generally speaking, deserves the support of the House. However, I believe that these questions need to be answered before this bill receives final approval, to ensure that it will be administered in a way consistent with the general public interest and thereby in the interests of all individual Canadians.
The purpose of a national government is to work for fair treatment of all groups in our society, whether they be identified in terms of region, occupation or patterns of expenditure. This bill is aimed at providing fairer treatment for a very important group in Canadian society. The government must go on to put in place its policy to ensure equally fair treatment with respect to food prices for the rest of the Canadian population in a way that is consistent with the commitment it gave so eloquently in the Speech from the Throne in February of last year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray). I thought it was too bad he was not a minister any more. It would have been very important for the hon. member to make such recommendations when he had certain powers.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on this bill which is highly significant for agriculture. It will be called the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It will bring changes in the definition of agricultural products, in the establishment of basic prices and will reduce from ten to five the years of evaluation prescribed in the former legislation. The bill also contains an interesting provision recommending an allowance for production costs. That is very important. The legislation also provides for regional stabilization, taking into account the sharp differences that may exist in the various areas. It is something the bill should correct. The law already protects certain products. We are told that the bill will allow the governor in council to add any agricultural commodity that will be deemed necessary. As a few members pointed out, that will puzzle the poeple. Of course we would have liked this bill to cover all agricultural products so that, notwithstanding the products concerned, producers will be sure of getting the protection of the law.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to quote certain remarks of the minister, who recognizes that agriculture is the foremost industry in Canada, that one job out of three surely depends on agriculture and that this bill will give the minister powers that none of his predecessors ever had. The minister also recognizes the importance of creating a climate of confidence for farmers, so that young people may stay on the farm. I believe those are excellent intentions. I noticed that the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard) said in his speech that it was a step in the right direction, and I believe we all agree as to the good intentions of the minister in respect of this bill although the same hon. member also pointed out quite
Agricultural Stabilization Act
rightly some concerns about certain commodities or methods of application.
Mr. Speaker, despite all the respect I have for the minister, the assurance of his good intentions, the efforts he made since he has been responsible for that department, I think it is also important to consider what happened generally-since 1968 as far as I am concerned-and what are the results of the government's agricultural policy. In the meantime, did agriculture gather extraordinary momentum? Is the farming community less concerned, more happy, better off? I think several questions remain unanswered.
I represent a riding quite interested in agriculture and in view of the unsatisfactory solutions that were put forward, it has been said, as the minister pointed out, that in recent years the government introduced several pieces of legislation in this House to improve the position of the agricultural sector, yet we are still faced with difficulties which do nothing to lessen the concerns of the farming community.
So, in view of that, the government having received briefs from several agricultural organizations, and in view of the importance of agriculture in this country, one must wonder whether the government did allocate the necessary funds. Indeed, recognizing the leading role of that industry, I think the Minister of Agriculture has failed to listen closely in cabinet when it came to apportioning the necessary votes to the various departments.
With respect to the milk industry, we know the position of milk producers. We must import rather large quantities of butter. The diminishing population of milk producers is disturbing, production costs have shot up beyond reason and, in this area as in others, there is a discouraging indebtedness, specially among young producers.
For instance I would like to point out to the minister that I read carefully the brief by the Canadian Federation of Dairy Producers which deals with the future policy to be applied by the minister and the government if they really are to make the effort needed by dairy producers especially. In other areas of production, expectations are similar; let me quote a letter by the Federation of Dairy Producers to members of parliament and to the minister in charge. I quote;
This is to underline the extreme importance of decisions to be taken by the government in the few days to come with regard to its policy for the 1975-76 dairy campaign ... We hope that, through those decisions, not only will the base price be set at a higher level within the stabilization program, but that an indexing provision will also be available to provide for accasional readjustments of that price.
Of course that indexing provision is important, but what is even more so is the basic level of revenues to which that index will apply. The present level of revenue is totally insufficient for that purpose; therefore the base price to be applied from April 1 and used for indexing revenues is a crucial decision. In its policy statement, the Canadian Federation of Dairy Producers requests an $11.62 per cwt. revenue for processed milk starting April 1. That level is substantially higher than the present $10.02 and shows the importance of a substantial increase in revenues as an indexing basis from April 1.
I therefore think for instance that it is important for the minister to take that recommendation by a leading Canadian industry into consideration.

I would also like to stress, Mr. Speaker, that I was personally very much in favour of that famous Bill C-176 which was expected to improve the situation of various categories of producers. When that marketing board would be implemented, we would manage to seriously cope with the shortcomings and difficulties of producers in general. We have had experience with eggs, as other members in the House have pointed out. We have had a very long study made by the board, in which it is recognized that there was a glaring lack of cooperation between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie). We could talk of poultry breeding and beef breeding. Everybody is well aware of these problems. There are the potato growers who are still meeting serious difficulties. The member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) spoke of the difficulties also met by the producers of maple sugar.
In the face of those unceasing difficulties, one can congratulate oneself and think that this legislation will correct the situation and calm down farmers or this class of producers. Personally, I have some reserves, as do other members in the House. And I wonder how deeply the government has thought and how much it has tried to control imports, which certainly seem to be a cause of trouble for our trade in agriculture.
During the commission's inquiry on the egg surplus, it was recognized there had been lack of control over imports. Today and yesterday, newspapers still reported massive imports. This is causing enormous hardship to our producers. Apparently, the minister does not wish to apply now stringent measures.
Under the bill, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has exceptional powers when a problem arises concerning a Canadian commodity. For that reason, Canadian farming is still undermined. Other producers are concerned. They wonder what the government is going to do. Some members indicated that the government had increased farm loans, that it had introduced longer repayment terms. They did not mention interest rates, almost prohitive for young farmers. In 1968, the interest rate on farm loans was 5 per cent. The ceiling was removed so that the market rate could be changed. A federal commission was established to get the facts about farming. That commission submitted reports informing us on an outdated situation.
In my opinion, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce deserves severe warning in the face of his inaction on imports and his lack of interest in problems now faced by the Minister of Agriculture. This makes things harder for the latter, because I feel he is looking for valid answers to farming problems. Producers hope the minister will be acting soon, because he has the power to control imports, which have enormously unsettling effects on our markets.
I would also like to emphasize the need for measures to preserve our agricultural area. There may have been a lack of coordination between the departments responsible for agriculture in general and already, Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing worldwide famine. It is therefore up to us to hurry up and make this industry efficient and more productive than ever before. We should not necessarily limit thoughts to available credits. I know that the government

has found extraordinary funds to simplify the work of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
To come back to the importance of the agricultural industry in our economy, I believe that this industry also deserves particular attention. This is what has been lacking, as well as the interest of the cabinet in general, as concerns the necessary credits which would have allowed the minister responsible to meet certain demands. We have also often emphasized the lack of control over the cost of feed and farm machinery. We are learning more about this every day. I want to repeat these things in the House because we hear comments from farmers who are very worried and wonder when costs will stop going up so that we may finally have the stabilization suggested today by the minister in his bill.
We should not forget the consumer in all this. I was listening a while ago to the hon. member for Windsor West who was asking that any farming policy be geared to the interest of the consumer. He was wondering how the consumer would pay the cost. Of course, the consumer deserves the respect of those who must represent his policy and he must also know that the price for the survival of the farming class will have to be paid. I believe that the government should inform the consumer about the minimum that the producer must obtain, while investigating seriously the middlemen. Finally, what is important is that the producer gets an absolutely necessary income. I wonder when the government will start holding a little investigation on the middlemen, that is individuals who stand between the producer, who must get a minimum income, and the consumer who must also pay a minimum price for that product. I believe there is a gap between those two and we must conduct a serious study to find out who enjoys the best profits.
Right now it is not the farmer who makes fantastic profits and, taking into account the consumer's purchasing power, we have the responsibility to insure them quality products at reasonable prices.
As members of parliament, we could require the government and its responsible agencies to pay special attention to the middlemen who could have taken some advantage from time to time of any particular situation.
Mr. Speaker, on the whole we recognize that this legislation is a step in the right direction, as one of my hon. colleagues said last week. We do not intend to oppose an improving measure and we also hope that the minister will be able to give the answers to some questions asked during this debate. For example, the hon. member for Windsor West asked several questions. I think they were all very relevant and interesting. Personally, I would have liked this legislation to give more assurance to the producers who make up the so-called farming industry.
As to the escalation formula which seems to be applicable in as much as we provide for increases in input costs, we do favour it because it will solve the problem of the continuous increase in input costs. The only thing we still have to know is to what extent the government will be able to assure us some control over the increase in the input costs which unbalance any legislation which could seem proper today but which would quickly become out-of-date as the increase in those costs has gone unchecked too long.

Mr. Speaker, I will merely make those few comments acknowledging the import of that legislation and hoping that the minister will bring some amendments when it is under consideration in committee so that all producers may profit by stabilization while being assured of a minimum price.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments in the bill before us to stabilize farm income are not very important. Basically, they do four things: they revise the named commodities in the legislation, they add a few commodities and take out a few, they shorten the stabilization period for the base price from ten years to five years, and they increase the floor for the basic minimums from 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the previous five-year average. Also, there is a clause in the bill allowing producers in certain areas or provinces, one by one, to opt into the program and to supplement the legislation before the House.
The reason I say the amendments before us are not really important is that last year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had four stabilization programs in which the minimums were above the minimum in this legislation. The bill before us provides floors-and I am sure that we are all happy with those floors-but it does not provide ceilings, and any program the minister might introduce could contain a floor that is above the ones we are considering today. So I suggest to the House that we should deal with this bill expeditiously. It will not create any fundamental or basic changes in the agricultural economy; it will just increase the benefits of the stabilization plan that we have. In other words, it is not a bill that is drastically important because it does not create any fundamental changes.
I want to mention six different areas about which I have questions and of which I hope the minister will take note. I do this because I think the agricultural community will be facing real problems. We have known for some time that beef farmers have been in trouble. The prices they receive for their commodities are much too low to allow them a decent standard of living. We know also that grain prices are falling, production costs are escalating, and as part of the world economy farmers will be facing difficult times.
I say that because I gather that on both sides of the House there is a feeling among members representing urban communities in particular that farmers have done very well in the last few years and that we should not be so concerned about them but, instead, we should turn our attention to other sectors of the economy. I want to remind hon. members that agriculture is the backbone of our economy and that although grain farmers in the last two or three years have not done badly, there are storm clouds on the horizon and we should turn our attention to them in particular.
The bill before us includes a whole series of commodities except western grain. We will be dealing with legislation on grain stabilization in the future. The first point I wish to mention to the minister is that of course I am happy to see him bring up the base price from 80 per cent
Agricultural Stabilization Act
of the previous ten-year average to 90 per cent of the previous five-year average. If we stabilize the price of commodities at 90 per cent of the previous five-year average, the farmer will fall behind economically because of general inflation in the economy.
There is every indication that inflation will increase rather than decrease, and if we stabilize the price the farmer will obtain at the previous five-year average, he will fall behind in economic terms. In order to counteract this, the minister has included a cost of production index. What worries me is that the definition of this index is left to the governor in council. What does the minister mean by "cost of production index"? Does he mean the whole cost in terms of fuel, fertilizer, machinery, and so on, that goes into producing a bushel of wheat, growing a heifer, growing a hog, or producing poultry?
I would like to hear the minister elaborate on what he means by "cost of production index," because even if we stabilize farm income at 90 per cent of the previous five-year average and put in a cost of production index, it might not be adequate. In fact, we would be stabilizing farm income downward from the economists' point of view. One could easily stabilize farm income at 100 per cent of the previous five-year average and still find the farmers falling behind. For example, are farmers' wages taken into consideration in the cost of production index? If they are, then the index might accurately reflect the true cost of production. That point should be clarified because this matter is left to the regulations. That is the most important part of the bill with which we are dealing.
The other point which I should like to mention to the minister is that there are still some commodities left out of the bill, and I wonder why. I am thinking particularly of oil seeds produced in western Canada. Why are they left out when western soybeans are in the bill? The third point I wanted to mention-and this is very important to my region-is that deficiency payments to be made under this plan are to be based on national averages for the commodities listed, but often there are regional or provincial fluctuations which have a bearing on what the farmer should be getting in terms of deficiency payments.
Let me give one example. In the region from which I come, namely, east central Saskatchewan, last year grain farmers encountered real difficulties in terms of weather. We had a very late spring, so the crop was put in late; then we had an early frost which froze the grain before it ripened. As a result, the farmer had a lower yield and a lower quality of grain in terms of grade and weight. We were below the average in the Wheat Board area. If deficiency payments were based on national averages, probably farmers in my area would not get any or, if they got them, their payments would be the same as those made in southern Saskatchewan where there was a higher yield of grain of a better grade, for which they got a better price.
Therefore, the minister should consider accepting amendments which would allow for greater regional flexibility. There is, for instance, the Peace River country of Alberta and the area of northern Saskatchewan north of my area where farmers experienced severe problems with weather during the growing season. If there is no flexibility in the legislation, farmers in some regions may be seriously affected.
